title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to manipulate the training or retrieval data that AI chatbots draw on when answering questions. A website presenting itself as a neutral research institution published a large volume of text structured to match the kinds of queries users submit to chatbots, using academic formatting and citations to legitimate sources while consistently framing contested events in a particular direction. The failure mode is not a malfunction of the AI systems themselves but an exploitation of their dependence on web-accessible text, which they have no native means of vetting for institutional authenticity.

The operation worked at the input layer of AI deployment, before any model reasoning occurs. Catching it would have required either verification of the publishing institution's legal existence or detection of coordinated bulk publication patterns, neither of which current chatbot pipelines are designed to perform automatically. The volume and speed of publication, 124 reports in eight days, is itself a signal that automated or semi-automated content generation was used to saturate the information environment quickly.

What is not established is whether any specific chatbot's outputs were durably changed by this content, or whether any AI company was aware of or complicit in the operation. The reporting describes the intent and mechanism of the campaign, not a confirmed measurable effect on model behavior.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

An Israeli-funded organization called the Hanover Institute for Public Policy, which does not appear to exist as a legal entity, created a fake think tank website designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots. Between August 6 and 14, the site published 124 reports totaling over 560,000 words framed as neutral research, covering topics including Israeli military actions, Palestinian casualties, and genocide allegations. The reports were structured as questions users might ask chatbots and used academic formatting with citations to legitimate sources, but consistently presented information in ways that defended Israel and suggested claims could not be verified without court rulings. The operation was part of a larger Israeli government campaign financed through European advertising firm Havas Media and routed through multiple American contractors.

The broader effort involves tens of millions of dollars in spending, including $15 million to a company run by former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale. Israeli officials have expressed frustration that despite substantial spending, American public opinion has turned sharply against Israel, with polling showing record opposition particularly among younger Americans. Researchers noted that while the campaign may successfully influence chatbot responses, it has failed to shift actual public opinion, suggesting the government views a political problem as purely a marketing challenge.
